cards.q: Do you agree? 'Primacy only ever requires a national court to disapply conflicting national measures; it can never require it to declare a national decision null and void.' (2 points)
cards.a:
No – disapplication is the rule, nullity an exception.
• Rule: the national rule is not non-existent, only disapplied; it still governs cases outside EU law (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97).
• Exception: a decision of a body that is no independent tribunal established by law (Art 47 Charter) must be declared null and void where essential for primacy, despite legal certainty (W.Ż., C-487/19; AW 'T', C-225/22).

cards.q: Describe how the German Federal Constitutional Court's ultra vires review developed from Maastricht to PSPP, and state the Court of Justice's position on such review. (3 points)
cards.a:
The BVerfG asserted, then restricted, then used ultra vires review; the CJEU rejects it.
• Maastricht (1993): review whether EU acts respect conferred powers (Art 5(2) TEU).
• Honeywell (2010): only manifest excess, highly significant for the competence structure, after a reference to the CJEU (Art 267 TFEU).
• PSPP (2020): ECB bond-buying (attacked as monetary financing, Art 123 TFEU) and CJEU's Weiss (C-493/17) held ultra vires – no proportionality review (Art 5(4) TEU).
• CJEU: only it invalidates EU acts (Foto-Frost, 314/85); constitutional courts are bound (RS, C-430/21).

cards.q: Do all Member States accept the primacy of EU law? On what grounds, and within what limits? (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes, assuming the Union stays within its competences – but on different grounds; AT, CZ, DK, FR, DE, IT, ES reserve constitutional limits; dispute: who decides them.
• Grounds: Costa v ENEL reasoning, or their own constitution (Art 23 German Basic Law; Austria: accession = total revision, Art 44(3) B-VG, referendum 1994).
• Limits (integration-proof core): fundamental rights (Solange), ultra vires (Maastricht, Honeywell, PSPP), identity (BVerfG Lisbon 2009, Art 79(3) Basic Law).
• CJEU: primacy also over constitutions (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70); identity only within EU law, Art 4(2) TEU.

cards.q: Describe the hierarchy of norms as the Court of Justice sees it. Why do national constitutional courts add a further layer on top, and how are primacy, ultra vires and competence connected? (3 points)
cards.a:
For the CJEU primary law is the apex; constitutional courts put their integration-proof core above it, having accepted primacy only for a Union within its powers.
• CJEU pyramid: primary law (Treaties, Charter, general principles) → international agreements (Art 216(2) TFEU) → secondary → tertiary law (Arts 290/291 TFEU) → national law, incl. constitutions.
• Circle: primacy → integration-proof core → ultra vires → competence (Art 5(2) TEU) → decided by EU law → primacy.
• Open: who has the last word – CJEU (Art 19(1) TEU) or constitutional courts.

cards.q: What is the difference between direct applicability and direct effect of EU law? Is every directly applicable provision also directly effective? Why (not)? (2 points)
cards.a:
No – every directly effective provision is directly applicable, but not vice versa.
• Direct applicability: part of the national legal order without transposition, e.g. regulations, Art 288(2) TFEU.
• Direct effect: confers a right invocable before national courts – clear, precise, unconditional (Van Gend en Loos, 26/62).
• Example: a regulation obliging states to create an authority – directly applicable, not directly effective.

cards.q: Mr Ratti's Italian firm produced solvents and varnishes. He labelled them according to two directives instead of the stricter Italian law and was prosecuted. The deadline of the solvents directive had expired without Italy implementing it; the deadline of the varnishes directive had not yet expired. Can Ratti rely on each directive as a defence? Why may individuals rely on directives at all? (3 points)
cards.a:
Solvents: yes, vertical direct effect after the deadline; varnishes: no, deadline not expired (Ratti, 148/78).
• Rule: a directive binds the state only as to the result (Art 288(3) TFEU) – no direct effect; exception: vertical direct effect (Van Duyn, 41/74).
• Conditions: clear, precise, unconditional + implementation error + deadline expired.
• Application: solvents – Italy may not apply its stricter law against Ratti; varnishes – early compliance gives no right.
• Rationale: effet utile; Art 267 TFEU; estoppel – the state may not rely on its own failure.

cards.q: Do you agree? 'A Member State that has failed to transpose a directive in time may rely on that directive against a private individual, for example to establish his criminal liability.' (2 points)
cards.a:
No – there is no inverse vertical direct effect, and a directive can never of itself determine or aggravate criminal liability.
• Kolpinghuis Nijmegen (80/86): the state cannot invoke an unimplemented directive against an individual; estoppel works only against the defaulting state.
• Berlusconi (C-387/02): no aggravation of criminal liability through a directive – legal certainty, nullum crimen and lex mitior (Art 49(1) Charter).

cards.q: Do all provisions of the Treaties have direct effect? Contrast Article 18 and Article 19 TFEU, and explain when a Treaty provision can be invoked against another private party. (3 points)
cards.a:
No – only clear, precise, unconditional provisions; horizontally only if they also govern relations between individuals.
• Art 18(1) TFEU: unconditional prohibition of nationality discrimination → directly effective.
• Art 19(1) TFEU: mere competence – the Council 'may take appropriate action' (unanimity, EP consent) → no direct effect.
• Vertical: any provision meeting the conditions, e.g. Art 30 TFEU (Van Gend en Loos).
• Horizontal: Art 157 TFEU (Defrenne II, 43/75), Arts 101/102 TFEU (BRT v SABAM, 127/73), Art 45 TFEU (Angonese, C-281/98).

cards.q: Do you agree? 'Once a Member State has transposed a directive, individuals can no longer rely on the directive itself before national courts.' (2 points)
cards.a:
No – normally the implementing law is relied on, but the directive remains invocable against the state if implementation fails.
• Implementation error suffices: none, incorrect, or correct transposition not applied correctly in practice (Marks & Spencer, C-62/00).
• Plus clear, precise, unconditional provision and expired deadline (Ratti, 148/78).
• Also: national law must be interpreted consistently with the directive (Von Colson, 14/83).

cards.q: What is the difference between the principle of equivalence and the principle of effectiveness? Can a national procedural rule that treats EU-law and domestic claims identically still infringe EU law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Both frame procedural autonomy; equivalence is relative, effectiveness absolute, so yes, an identically applied rule can still infringe EU law.
• Rewe (33/76), Comet (45/76), restated in Impact (C-268/06); basis Arts 4(3) and 19(1) second subpara TEU.
• Equivalence: rules for EU claims no less favourable than for similar domestic actions (closest domestic analogue).
• Effectiveness: exercise of EU rights must not be practically impossible or excessively difficult (Impact; softer than Rewe's 'impossible in practice'), even if domestic claims fare equally badly.
• Reasonable time limits pass (legal certainty).

cards.q: Describe how a national court proceeds when the national procedural rule governing a claim based on EU law appears to make that claim excessively difficult. (3 points)
cards.a:
It tests the rule against equivalence and effectiveness and, if it fails, interprets it in conformity or disapplies it.
• EU procedural rules (e.g. Arts 77 ff. GDPR) prevail; procedural autonomy is residual.
• Test: the rule's role in the whole procedure (Peterbroeck, C-312/93).
• Step 1: conforming interpretation (Art 4(3) TEU, Von Colson, 14/83).
• Step 2: otherwise disapply it of its own motion by virtue of primacy (Simmenthal, 106/77).
• Step 3: possibly a remedy directly under EU law (Art 4(3) TEU; interim relief: Factortame I, C-213/89).

cards.q: Does EU law oblige a national authority to reopen a final administrative decision that later turns out to rest on a misinterpretation of EU law? (3 points)
cards.a:
In principle no, because legal certainty protects finality, but exceptionally yes under the four cumulative Kühne & Heitz conditions (C-453/00), based on Art 4(3) TEU.
• (1) National law empowers the authority to reopen the decision.
• (2) The decision became final through a judgment of a court ruling at final instance.
• (3) That judgment rested on a misinterpretation of EU law adopted without a preliminary reference under Art 267(3) TFEU.
• (4) The person complained to the authority immediately after learning of the later CJEU ruling.

cards.q: What is meant by the 'incidental (horizontal) effect' of directives? Give two examples and explain why the Court of Justice regards it as compatible with the rule that directives have no horizontal direct effect. (3 points)
cards.a:
A directive relied on vertically, or to exclude a national rule, may adversely affect a private party without imposing an obligation on that party.
• Triangular situation: Delena Wells (C-201/02): EIA Directive invoked against the UK; the burden on the quarry owner is a permitted 'mere adverse repercussion'.
• Technical standards: CIA Security (C-194/94), Unilever (C-443/98): an unnotified national technical rule is inapplicable even between private parties.
• Compatible because the directive creates no obligation for the individual; it only removes a procedurally defective national rule (Marshall, Faccini Dori untouched).

cards.q: How can a directive become relevant in a dispute between private parties where it gives expression to a general principle of EU law or to a Charter right? (3 points)
cards.a:
The directive has no horizontal effect, but the general principle or Charter right it concretises applies between private parties, so the court must disapply conflicting national law.
• Mangold (C-144/04), Kücükdeveci (C-555/07): age non-discrimination is a general principle; Directive 2000/78 gives it concrete expression; no prior reference needed.
• The directive brings the case within the Charter's scope (Art 51(1)): Art 21 (Egenberger, C-414/16), Art 31(2) (Bauer, C-569/16), Art 47 with Directive 1999/70 (KL, C-715/20).
• Limit: the right must be sufficient in itself; Art 27 is not (AMS, C-176/12).

cards.q: When is a breach of EU law by a Member State 'sufficiently serious' for the purposes of state liability? (3 points)
cards.a:
When the Member State manifestly and gravely disregarded the limits on its discretion (Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III, C-46/93 and C-48/93).
• Factors: clarity and precision of the rule; discretion left; intentional breach; excusable error; contributing position of an EU institution.
• Little or no discretion: mere infringement may suffice (Hedley Lomas, C-5/94).
• Non-transposition by the deadline is per se serious (Dillenkofer, C-178/94).
• Always serious if persisting despite a CJEU judgment or settled case law; a defensible reading of an unclear directive is not (British Telecommunications, C-392/93).

cards.q: Do you agree? 'A Member State can be held liable under Francovich only where its legislature has failed to transpose a directive.' (3 points)
cards.a:
No: the State is liable for any sufficiently serious breach by any of its organs (Brasserie du Pêcheur, C-46/93 and C-48/93).
• Legislature: not only non-transposition (Francovich) but also legislation contrary to directly effective Treaty provisions (Brasserie/Factortame III).
• Administration: Hedley Lomas (C-5/94), Danske Slagterier (C-445/06).
• Judiciary at last instance: Köbler (C-224/01), only for a manifest infringement, e.g. disregarding Art 267(3) TFEU or clear case law.
• The State cannot plead its internal division of powers; a region or public-law body may pay (Konle, C-302/97; Haim, C-424/97).

cards.q: Is state liability available only where the infringed EU provision has no direct effect? Why (not)? (2 points)
cards.a:
No: state liability is the 'necessary corollary' of direct effect and applies whether or not the provision is directly effective (Brasserie du Pêcheur).
• Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90): the directive lacked direct effect (unclear who pays), yet damages were due.
• Brasserie: the breached Arts 30 and 52 EEC (now 34, 49 TFEU) were directly effective; direct effect does not compensate past loss.

cards.q: Do you agree? 'Where a consumer cannot recover from his supplier a tax charged contrary to a directive, because directives have no horizontal direct effect, EU law leaves him without a remedy.' (2 points)
cards.a:
No: if the consumer cannot rely on the directive against the supplier, effectiveness requires a claim directly against the State (Gabel Industria Tessile, C-316/22).
• Art 288(3) TFEU: no disapplication against the private supplier, unless national law allows it (Thelen Technopark, C-261/20) or the supplier is an emanation of the State (Foster).
• Recovery only via the supplier would be practically impossible; alternatively Francovich damages.

cards.q: Give an overview of the four main procedures before the Court of Justice of the European Union: who may bring them, against whom or what, and which court decides? (4 points)
cards.a:
Preliminary reference (Art 267), infringement (Arts 258–260), annulment (Arts 263–264), failure to act (Art 265 TFEU).
• Art 267: only national courts ask, on interpretation of EU law or validity of EU acts; Court of Justice (some areas General Court, Art 256(3)).
• Arts 258/259: Commission or a Member State against a Member State; Court of Justice only; declaratory, sanctions under Art 260.
• Art 263: Member States, institutions, individuals (263(4)) against binding EU acts within two months (263(6)); act void (Art 264).
• Art 265: same applicants against an institution's failure to act, after a call to act.
• Individuals: General Court (Art 256(1)), incl. damages (Arts 268, 340(2)); appeal to Court of Justice.

cards.q: Which of these questions may a national court refer to the Court of Justice under Article 267(1) TFEU? (a) Is Article 34 TFEU valid? (b) How is a Commission recommendation to be interpreted? (c) Is a provision of an association agreement concluded by the Union with a third country directly effective? (d) Is a provision of an Austrian Land statute compatible with the Austrian Federal Constitution? (3 points)
cards.a:
(b), (c) yes; (a), (d) no — Art 267(1) TFEU: interpretation of the Treaties; validity and interpretation of acts of EU institutions, bodies, offices or agencies.
• (a) Art 267(1)(a): primary law is only interpreted, never reviewed for validity.
• (b) Covers non-binding acts too; national courts must take recommendations into account (Grimaldi C-322/88).
• (c) Agreements concluded by the Union are acts of the institutions and an integral part of EU law (Haegeman 181/73).
• (d) National law is outside Art 267; the Court interprets only EU law.

cards.q: Which of the following may make a preliminary reference under Article 267 TFEU, and by which criteria? (a) an Austrian Landesverwaltungsgericht; (b) an arbitral tribunal set up by contract between two companies; (c) the director of a national tax administration deciding on objections against assessments issued by his own administration; (d) the Austrian Verfassungsgerichtshof. (4 points)
cards.a:
(a) yes, (b) no, (c) no, (d) yes — 'court or tribunal' is an autonomous EU concept; the national label is irrelevant.
• Vaassen (61/65), Dorsch Consult (C-54/96): established by law, permanent, compulsory jurisdiction, inter partes procedure, applies rules of law, independent.
• (a) Administrative court meets all criteria → may refer; must refer only if no judicial remedy lies against its decision (Art 267(3)).
• (b) Jurisdiction rests on the parties' agreement, not compulsory → no (Nordsee 102/81); a state court reviewing the award may refer.
• (c) Not independent of the administration it reviews → no (Corbiau C-24/92).
• (d) Constitutional court → may, as last instance must, refer (Seitlinger C-594/12).

cards.q: Do you agree? 'In a preliminary ruling the Court of Justice may declare an Austrian statute incompatible with EU law and therefore void, and it thereby decides the case for the referring court.' (2 points)
cards.a:
No — the Court only interprets EU law (or rules on EU acts' validity); the referring court decides the case.
• Art 267(1) TFEU: no jurisdiction over national law; it rules whether EU law 'precludes legislation such as…'.
• Bound by the ruling, the national court applies it and disapplies the statute (Simmenthal 106/77).
• Not void, only inapplicable (IN.CO.GE.'90 C-10/97); legislator must repeal it.

cards.q: Do you agree? 'A preliminary ruling binds only the referring court and applies only from the day it is delivered.' (3 points)
cards.a:
No — it reaches beyond the case (erga omnes effect) and as a rule applies ex tunc.
• Binds all courts in the same case; other courts follow it or refer again (Da Costa 28–30/62).
• Invalidity ruling: every national court treats the act as invalid (International Chemical Corporation 66/80).
• Ex tunc: it states what the rule always meant → covers earlier relationships (Denkavit Italiana 61/79).
• Only the Court, in that same ruling, may limit temporal effects: good faith + risk of serious difficulties (Defrenne II 43/75).

cards.q: Do you agree? (a) A lower court that, under national procedural law, is bound by the legal assessment of a higher court on remand may no longer refer. (b) An appeal court may set aside a lower court's order for reference. (c) A judge may face disciplinary proceedings for an unnecessary reference. (3 points)
cards.a:
No to all three — referring is the national court's sole discretion; national law cannot restrict it.
• (a) Rheinmühlen (166/73), Elchinov (C-173/09): it may refer and must disregard a higher court's view contrary to EU law.
• (b) Cartesio (C-210/06): an appeal court cannot amend or set aside the order; only the referring court may withdraw it.
• (c) Miasto Łowicz (C-558/18), IS (C-564/19): disciplinary proceedings for a reference breach Art 267 TFEU and Art 19(1) subpara 2 TEU.
• Nor may priority constitutional review block it (Melki C-188/10).

cards.q: Is the Commission obliged to bring infringement proceedings, and can a citizen whose complaint it ignores force it to? Which defences of a Member State does the Court typically reject? (4 points)
cards.a:
No — Art 258 TFEU gives the Commission discretion ('may'); a complainant cannot force it.
• Discretion whether and when to start and whether to go to Court after the reasoned opinion.
• Star Fruit (247/87): refusal cannot be challenged under Arts 263 or 265 TFEU → national courts (direct effect, primacy, Francovich); at most an Ombudsman complaint (Art 228 TFEU).
• Objective procedure, no fault: the State answers for all organs, even parliament (Commission v Belgium 77/69).
• Rejected: internal constitutional or practical difficulties; other States' breaches (Commission v Luxembourg and Belgium 90–91/63); late compliance — the reasoned-opinion deadline decides.

cards.q: Which courts are obliged to refer under Article 267(3) TFEU? Must a national appeal court refer if its judgment can be challenged before the supreme court only with leave? (2 points)
cards.a:
Courts whose decision cannot be challenged in the specific case (concrete approach); an appeal court subject to leave need not refer.
• Concrete, not abstract: even a lower court must refer if no remedy exists in that case (Costa v ENEL 6/64, non-appealable small claim).
• Lyckeskog (C-99/00): an appeal requiring leave is a remedy → the supreme court must refer when deciding on leave.

cards.q: Under what conditions is the Union liable in damages for unlawful conduct of its institutions? Before which court and within what time limit must the action be brought? (3 points)
cards.a:
Art 340(2) TFEU, if three conditions are met; action before the General Court (Arts 268, 256(1) TFEU) within five years (Art 46 Statute).
• Breach of a rule of law intended to confer rights on individuals.
• Sufficiently serious: manifest and grave disregard of the limits of discretion; with little or no discretion a mere infringement may suffice (Bergaderm C-352/98 P, same test as Brasserie du Pêcheur).
• Actual damage and a direct causal link.
• Autonomous action, no prior annulment needed (Lütticke 4/69).

cards.q: In infringement proceedings, the Commission fears that a Member State's new law sending Supreme Court judges into early retirement will cause irreparable harm before judgment. Can it obtain interim relief from the Court of Justice, on what conditions, and what if the State ignores the order? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes — the Court may order any necessary interim measures in a pending case, also against a Member State (Art 279 TFEU).
• Only once the Art 258 action is brought (Art 160(2) RP).
• Prima facie case, urgency (serious, irreparable damage), balance of interests.
• Poland: C-619/18 R suspended judges' retirement rules; C-204/21 R the Disciplinary Chamber — ignored → €1m daily penalty.

cards.q: (a) Can a judgment of the General Court be challenged, on what grounds and within what time limit? (b) Do you agree: 'Only the Court of Justice can give preliminary rulings'? (3 points)
cards.a:
(a) Yes, by appeal to the Court of Justice on points of law only; (b) no longer — since 1 October 2024 the General Court decides references in specific areas.
• Art 256(1) subpara 2 TFEU, Art 56 Statute: within two months, by the unsuccessful party.
• Grounds (Art 58 Statute): lack of competence, procedural breach, infringement of EU law; no review of facts; quash and decide or refer back (Art 61 Statute).
• Art 256(3) TFEU, Art 50b Statute: VAT, excise duties, customs, tariff classification, passenger rights, emissions trading.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Describe how an action for annulment under Art 263 TFEU is examined: what is checked at the admissibility stage, what at the merits stage, and what follows if the action succeeds? (4 points)
cards.a:
Admissible if a binding EU act is challenged in time by an applicant with standing and interest; well founded if an Art 263(2) TFEU ground applies.
• Court: General Court for individuals (Art 256(1) TFEU); Court of Justice where Art 51 Statute reserves it (mainly Member States v Parliament/Council).
• Act: intended to produce legal effects vis-à-vis third parties (Art 263(1); ERTA, 22/70); defendant = its EU author.
• Standing: privileged 263(2), semi-privileged 263(3), non-privileged 263(4); two months, 263(6).
• Grounds: lack of competence, breach of an essential procedural requirement, of the Treaties or rules applying them, misuse of powers.
• Success: void ex tunc, erga omnes (Art 264(1)); effects maintainable (264(2)); compliance Art 266.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: A state-aid beneficiary was informed of a Commission decision ordering recovery of the aid and undoubtedly could have challenged it under Art 263(4) TFEU, but let the two-month period expire. In the national recovery proceedings it claims the decision is invalid and asks for a preliminary reference. Will it succeed? (3 points)
cards.a:
No: a party that undoubtedly had standing cannot, after expiry, contest validity before a national court (TWD Textilwerke Deggendorf, C-188/92).
• Art 263(6) TFEU: two months from publication, notification or knowledge; then the decision is definitive for it (legal certainty).
• An Art 267(1)(b) validity reference would circumvent the time limit; the national court treats the decision as valid.
• Art 277 TFEU does not help: only general acts, only before EU courts.
• If standing was doubtful (e.g. regulation), a reference stays open (Accrington Beef, C-241/95).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: What is the plea of illegality under Art 277 TFEU? Is it an independent action, and how does its effect differ from that of an annulment judgment? (3 points)
cards.a:
An incidental plea in pending EU-court proceedings, not an independent action; it makes the underlying general act inapplicable in that case only.
• Art 277 TFEU: even after the Art 263(6) period, any party may plead the Art 263(2) grounds against a general act at issue.
• Wöhrmann (31/62): no independent action; Simmenthal v Commission (92/78): also acts with regulation-like effects.
• Effect: inter partes; the measure based on it falls, the general act stays valid erga omnes (no annulment).
• National courts: Art 267 validity reference (Foto-Frost, 314/85).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: The Plaumann formula denies most individuals direct access to the EU courts against acts of general application. Does this violate the right to effective judicial protection (Art 47 Charter)? Why (not)? (3 points)
cards.a:
No (CJEU): the Treaties form a complete system of remedies; individuals are protected indirectly via national courts and Art 267 TFEU.
• Les Verts (294/83), UPA (C-50/00 P): Arts 263, 277 or Art 267 validity references; only the CJEU invalidates EU acts (Foto-Frost).
• Art 19(1) subpara 2 TEU: Member States must provide sufficient remedies (Art 47 CFR).
• UPA, Jégo-Quéré (C-263/02 P): relaxing Plaumann needs Treaty amendment.
• Lisbon added regulatory acts to Art 263(4); Inuit (C-583/11 P): legislative acts stay under Plaumann; Art 47 changes no Treaty remedy.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Are the rights in the Charter of Fundamental Rights absolute? Describe the requirements for limiting a Charter right and how the Charter relates to the ECHR in this respect. (4 points)
cards.a:
Most Charter rights can be limited under Art 52(1) CFR; a few are absolute (Art 1 dignity, Art 4 torture and inhuman treatment).
• Art 52(1): limitation (1) provided for by law, (2) respecting the essence of the right, (3) proportionate: necessary and genuinely meeting an objective of general interest recognised by the Union or protecting others' rights.
• Example: Digital Rights Ireland (C-293/12): Data Retention Directive invalid, disproportionate interference with Arts 7, 8 CFR.
• Art 52(3): ECHR-corresponding rights have the same meaning and scope; Union law may protect more (ECHR = floor, Art 53).
• Art 52(5): 'principles' (e.g. Art 37 environment) are justiciable only for interpreting and reviewing implementing acts.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Is the EU bound by the European Convention on Human Rights? Why (not)? (3 points)
cards.a:
Not formally (no accession yet), but ECHR rights bind it in substance.
• Art 6(2) TEU + Protocol No 8: duty to accede; Art 218(6)(a)(ii), (8) TFEU: Parliament consent, Council unanimity.
• Opinion 2/94: no competence pre-Lisbon; Opinion 2/13: draft breaches autonomy of EU law (mutual trust, Art 344 TFEU, CFSP).
• Art 6(3) TEU: ECHR rights are general principles; Art 52(3) CFR: corresponding Charter rights share their meaning and scope.
• Member States stay bound; Bosphorus (ECtHR 2005): equivalent protection presumed when implementing EU law without discretion.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Do you agree? Justify briefly. (a) The Charter allows the Union to legislate on any fundamental right it guarantees. (b) Since the Charter became binding, unwritten general principles of fundamental rights are obsolete. (c) Protocol No 30 exempts Poland from the Charter. (3 points)
cards.a:
All three statements are false.
• (a) Art 6(1) subpara 2 TEU, Art 51(2) CFR: the Charter does not extend EU competences; legislation still needs a Treaty legal basis (conferral, Art 5(2) TEU).
• (b) Art 6(3) TEU: ECHR rights and common constitutional traditions remain general principles of EU law, alongside the Charter and filling its gaps.
• (c) N.S. (C-411/10): Protocol No 30 is not an opt-out; the Charter applies in Poland. It only clarifies, e.g. Title IV rights are justiciable only as national law provides (Art 1(2)).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: Case — Nordia leaves: after a referendum, Member State Nordia decides to leave the Union. (a) Describe the withdrawal procedure under Art 50 TEU, including the majorities. (b) What happens if no agreement is reached? (c) After a change of government Nordia wants to stay — can it withdraw its notification unilaterally? (d) Could Nordia later rejoin? (4 points)
cards.a:
Unilateral right exercised by notifying the European Council; the Treaties cease when the withdrawal agreement enters into force or after two years.
• (a) Art 50(1)–(2) TEU: decision under Nordia's constitutional requirements → notification → European Council guidelines → Union negotiates (Art 218(3) TFEU).
• Council concludes by QMV under Art 238(3)(b) TFEU (72% of remaining members, 65% of their population) after EP consent; Nordia excluded (Art 50(4)).
• (b) Art 50(3): cliff edge two years after notification unless the European Council, with Nordia, unanimously extends.
• (c) Yes: unequivocal, unconditional written revocation before withdrawal takes effect (Wightman, C-621/18).
• (d) Only via a new Art 49 TEU application (Art 50(5)).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: Morocco applied for membership in 1987; today a Balkan state with a fragile, government-controlled judiciary applies. Which conditions must an applicant meet under Art 49 TEU, and how does the procedure work up to membership? (4 points)
cards.a:
Only a European state respecting and promoting the Art 2 TEU values may apply; Council unanimity, EP consent and ratification by all are required.
• 'European' state (Art 49(1) TEU): hence Morocco's rejection.
• Copenhagen criteria ('conditions of eligibility', Art 49(1) last sentence): political (democracy, rule of law, human rights, minorities), economic (market economy), acquis; plus EU absorption capacity.
• Government-controlled judiciary breaches the rule of law (Art 2 TEU, political criterion) → no accession until reformed.
• Procedure: application to the Council; EP and national parliaments notified; Commission consulted; EP consent (majority of component members); Council unanimity.
• Art 49(2): accession treaty with the Member States, ratified by all under their constitutional requirements.

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: At its next summit the European Council wants (i) to elect the Belgian Prime Minister as its President by simple majority for five years while he stays Prime Minister, and (ii) to adopt a directive on asylum procedures. Assess both plans. How does the European Council normally decide, and what are its main roles? (4 points)
cards.a:
Both unlawful: the President needs QMV, serves 2.5 years and may hold no national office; the European Council cannot legislate.
• Art 15(5) TEU: elected by QMV for two and a half years, renewable once.
• Art 15(6) last subpara: no national office → he must resign as Prime Minister (Charles Michel, 2019).
• Art 15(1): impetus and political priorities, 'shall not exercise legislative functions' → directive only by EP and Council in the OLP.
• Art 15(4): consensus unless the Treaties provide otherwise (e.g. QMV in Art 17(7) TEU).
• Roles: political direction, recruiting body (Commission President, HR Art 18(1)), arbiter, constitutional architect (Art 48), external representation; institution only since Lisbon (Art 13(1)).

cards.topic: EU Institutions I — European Council and Commission
cards.q: Case — Commissioner Kovač publicly declares that she votes in the College as instructed by her home government. The Commission President wants her out; her Member State insists on keeping 'its' Commissioner. (a) Is her conduct lawful? (b) How can she be removed? (c) Must every Member State have a Commissioner? (d) How does the College take decisions? (4 points)
cards.a:
Unlawful — Commissioners must be completely independent; the President can demand her resignation.
• (a) Art 17(3) TEU, Art 245(1) TFEU: no instructions from any government; Member States must respect that independence.
• (b) Art 17(6) last subpara TEU: she must resign if the President so requests; otherwise the Court of Justice may compulsorily retire her on application of Council or Commission (Arts 245(2), 247 TFEU); EP censure only against the whole College (Art 234 TFEU).
• (c) Art 17(5) TEU foresaw two thirds from 2014; the European Council unanimously kept one per Member State (Decision 2013/272/EU) — but no national mandate.
• (d) Collegiality, no department principle; majority of its Members (Art 250 TFEU).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Case — Land Tirol: the Commission decides that aid granted by the Land Tirol to a ski-lift operator is incompatible with the internal market and must be recovered. (a) Can Tirol bring an annulment action as a privileged applicant, like Austria? (b) If not, how and before which court can it sue? (c) Does Art 265 TFEU distinguish privileged and semi-privileged applicants? (3 points)
cards.a:
No — regions are not 'Member States'; Tirol is a non-privileged applicant under Art 263(4) TFEU before the General Court.
• (a) Art 263(2) 'Member State' = central government only (Région wallonne, C-95/97; Regione Siciliana, C-15/06 P) → only Austria privileged; EESC, EIB, European Council also non-privileged.
• (b) Direct and individual concern (Plaumann): decision concerns its own aid, forces recovery (Vlaams Gewest, T-214/95); two months (Art 263(6)); General Court (Art 256(1)).
• (c) No: all Member States and institutions are fully privileged (Art 265(1)); others only under Art 265(3).

cards.q: Case — Directive 2019/X gives consumers 14 days to withdraw from doorstep contracts. The transposition deadline expired a year ago; Tarvia has not transposed it, and an older Tarvian statute expressly grants only 7 days. Ms Ada withdrew 10 days after signing a doorstep contract with Vendo Ltd, a privately owned company, which now sues her in a Tarvian court for the price. Can Ada rely on the directive against Vendo? Work through the possible routes in the order you would use them. (5 points)
cards.a:
No: a directive cannot of itself impose obligations on a private party (Art 288(3) TFEU; Marshall I; Faccini Dori C-91/92), and no workaround helps.
• 1. Broad 'state' (Foster C-188/89): Vendo is private, no state control or special powers → fails.
• 2. Consistent interpretation (Von Colson; Marleasing, also older law): reading the express 7 days as 14 is contra legem → fails.
• 3. Incidental/triangular effect (Delena Wells; CIA Security, Unilever): no state measure, no unnotified technical rule → fails.
• 4. General principle/Charter right (Mangold; Kücükdeveci; Art 47 CFR, KL C-715/20): consumer protection (Art 38 CFR) is a mere principle (Art 52(5) CFR) → fails.
• 5. Viamex Agrar: no regulation conditions a benefit on the directive → fails; only Francovich damages against Tarvia (non-transposition per se serious, Dillenkofer).

cards.q: Case — Tarvia had to transpose Directive X by 1 January 2025. The Commission sends a letter of formal notice in March 2025, then a reasoned opinion on non-transposition with a deadline of 30 September 2025. Tarvia transposes on 15 November 2025. In its application to the Court the Commission also complains that Tarvia applies Article 7 of the directive incorrectly. (a) Describe the stages of the procedure. (b) Is the action still well founded? (c) Can the Court examine the Article 7 complaint? (3 points)
cards.a:
Well founded, but the Court cannot examine the Article 7 complaint.
• (a) Art 258 TFEU: informal contacts → letter of formal notice (observations) → reasoned opinion with deadline → Court of Justice.
• (b) Breach assessed at the reasoned-opinion deadline (30 September 2025); later transposition does not cure it → declaratory judgment (Art 260(1) TFEU); lump sum possible for a legislative directive (Art 260(3)).
• (c) Pre-litigation stage fixes the subject matter and protects the defence; application cannot exceed the reasoned opinion → Article 7 needs new proceedings.

cards.q: What are 'trilogues', why are almost all ordinary legislative acts now adopted at first reading, and why is this practice criticised? (2 points)
cards.a:
Trilogues are informal EP–Council–Commission negotiations whose compromise the formal readings then rubber-stamp.
• Not in Art 294 TFEU: EP adopts the agreed text as its first-reading position, Council approves it (Art 294(3)–(4)).
• First-reading adoption rose from 28% (1999–2004) to 89% (2014–2019); third reading fell from 22% to 1%.
• Criticism: transparency and legitimacy; trilogue documents must in principle be accessible (De Capitani, T-540/15).

cards.q: Case — Polonia lowers the retirement age of its Supreme Court judges with immediate effect and creates a disciplinary chamber controlled by the executive. Polonia argues that the organisation of its judiciary is a purely national competence and that the Charter does not apply because no EU law is being implemented. On what EU-law basis can the Commission challenge the reforms? (3 points)
cards.a:
Infringement action (Art 258 TFEU) for breach of Art 19(1) second subparagraph TEU: effective legal protection presupposes independent courts.
• Covers every national court that may rule on EU law, regardless of Art 51(1) CFR 'implementation' (ASJP, C-64/16).
• Judicial organisation is national competence but must respect EU law: the retirement reform breached Art 19(1) TEU (Commission v Poland, C-619/18), so did the disciplinary regime (C-791/19).
• Interim measures suspending the reforms (Art 279 TFEU).
• Concretises the rule of law (Art 2 TEU); read with Art 47 CFR.

cards.q: The Austrian Verwaltungsgerichtshof refers a question on the interpretation of a directive to the Court of Justice. Describe the course of the procedure up to the ruling: what happens to the national case, who is notified and may comment, and when can the Court dispense with the Advocate General's Opinion or rule by order? (3 points)
cards.a:
The VwGH stays its case; the Registrar notifies the interested persons, who have two months for observations.
• Art 23 Statute: parties, Member States, Commission, author institution; one round, no reply.
• Judge-Rapporteur and AG designated (Arts 15, 16 RoP); preliminary report (Art 59 RoP) decides formation, hearing, Opinion.
• No AG Opinion only if no new point of law (Art 20(5) Statute).
• Reasoned order if identical, clear from case law or beyond reasonable doubt (Art 99 RoP) or manifestly inadmissible (Art 53(2) RoP); else judgment binding the VwGH.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: A company invokes Article 1 (human dignity) and Article 17 (property) of the Charter; a Russian national living in Vienna invokes Article 39 (right to vote in European Parliament elections). Who holds Charter rights? Which types of rights does the Charter contain, and how does it differ from the ECHR in this respect? (3 points)
cards.a:
Natural and legal persons hold Charter rights, except highly personal rights (legal persons) and citizens' rights (non-citizens).
• Legal persons: property (Art 17), business (Art 16) yes; dignity (Art 1), life (Art 2) no → company only Art 17.
• Citizens' rights (Title V, e.g. Arts 39, 40, 45(1)) only for Union citizens → not the Russian.
• Three generations: civil/political, social (Title IV, e.g. Arts 31, 34), collective (Art 37 environment) — the ECHR essentially only the first.
• 'Principles' justiciable only via implementing acts (Art 52(5) CFR).

cards.q: When did Austria join the European Union, and together with which states? Outline the enlargement rounds from the six founding states to today's 27 Member States. (3 points)
cards.a:
Austria joined on 1 January 1995 together with Finland and Sweden (EU-15).
• Founders (ECSC 1951, Treaties of Rome 1957): Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands.
• 1973 Denmark, Ireland, UK; 1981 Greece; 1986 Spain, Portugal.
• 2004 ten states: Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia.
• 2007 Bulgaria, Romania; 2013 Croatia (EU-28).
• 2020 UK withdrew under Art 50 TEU → EU-27; candidates include Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans.

cards.q: Case — Lipa beer: Czech brewery Lipa lawfully makes and sells in Czechia a lager with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'; Austrian importer Hopfenhandel sells it in supermarkets and petrol-station shops. Austrian Beer Act: § 3 – 'Bier' only if brewed solely from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer may be sold at petrol stations. No EU harmonisation. An Austrian authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both. Austria invokes consumer expectations, health (rice beer 'less healthy') and drink-driving. (a) Which fundamental freedom is affected, where is it regulated, and does its scope apply? (2 points)
cards.a:
Free movement of goods (Art 28–37 TFEU); its scope applies.
• Goods: products with a money value, capable of trade (Commission v Italy, 7/68) – beer.
• Cross-border: Czech beer imported into Austria (Art 34; Union goods, Art 28(2)); importer's nationality irrelevant.
• Non-tariff rules, not duties/taxes (Art 30, 110).
• Addressee: Austria, all organs; no harmonisation → Art 34–36 apply; Art 34 directly effective.

cards.q: Case — Lipa beer: Czech brewery Lipa lawfully makes and sells in Czechia a lager with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'; Austrian importer Hopfenhandel sells it in supermarkets and petrol-station shops. Austrian Beer Act: § 3 – 'Bier' only if brewed solely from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer may be sold at petrol stations. No EU harmonisation. An Austrian authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both. Austria invokes consumer expectations, health (rice beer 'less healthy') and drink-driving. (b) Does § 3 restrict the free movement of goods? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes – § 3 is a product requirement (name/composition), hence an MEEQR (Art 34 TFEU), although it applies to all beer.
• Dassonville (8/74): trading rules capable of hindering intra-EU trade, directly or indirectly, actually or potentially.
• Cassis (120/78): dual burden – Lipa must change recipe or name for Austria (beer purity: Commission v Germany, 178/84).
• Product rule, not a Keck selling arrangement.

cards.q: Case — Lipa beer: Czech brewery Lipa lawfully makes and sells in Czechia a lager with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'; Austrian importer Hopfenhandel sells it in supermarkets and petrol-station shops. Austrian Beer Act: § 3 – 'Bier' only if brewed solely from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer may be sold at petrol stations. No EU harmonisation. An Austrian authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both. Austria invokes consumer expectations, health (rice beer 'less healthy') and drink-driving. (c) Assuming § 3 restricts the free movement of goods, can Austria justify it? (3 points)
cards.a:
No – § 3 is disproportionate and infringes Art 34 TFEU as applied to imported beer.
• Grounds: indistinctly applicable → Art 36 TFEU (health) and Cassis mandatory requirements (consumer protection); never economic protectionism.
• Consumers: labelling ('brewed with rice') is less restrictive; law may not crystallise consumer habits (Commission v Germany, 178/84).
• Health: Austria must prove a real risk; rice is ordinary food and the drink stays on sale under another name → incoherent.
• Burden on Austria → fine unlawful insofar as based on § 3.

cards.q: Case — Lipa beer: Czech brewery Lipa lawfully makes and sells in Czechia a lager with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'; Austrian importer Hopfenhandel sells it in supermarkets and petrol-station shops. Austrian Beer Act: § 3 – 'Bier' only if brewed solely from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer may be sold at petrol stations. No EU harmonisation. An Austrian authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both. Austria invokes consumer expectations, health (rice beer 'less healthy') and drink-driving. (d) Assess § 7 (ban on selling beer at petrol stations) under the free movement of goods. (2 points)
cards.a:
§ 7 is a Keck selling arrangement outside Art 34 TFEU; the fine stands to that extent.
• Keck (C-267/91): where/when/by whom rules escape Art 34 if applying to all traders and affecting domestic and imported goods alike, in law and fact.
• § 7: place of sale, all beer, equal effect.
• Otherwise (Gourmet, C-405/98) → MEEQR, justifiable (Art 36 health; road safety).

cards.q: Case — Lipa beer: Czech brewery Lipa lawfully makes and sells in Czechia a lager with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'; Austrian importer Hopfenhandel sells it in supermarkets and petrol-station shops. Austrian Beer Act: § 3 – 'Bier' only if brewed solely from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer may be sold at petrol stations. No EU harmonisation. An Austrian authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both. Austria invokes consumer expectations, health (rice beer 'less healthy') and drink-driving. Hopfenhandel appeals to the Landesverwaltungsgericht (revision to the VwGH possible), asking it to have the Court of Justice 'annul the Beer Act'. (e) May or must the court refer, is it bound by the request, and what can the Court of Justice do? (2 points)
cards.a:
It may (not must) refer on Art 34/36 TFEU, unbound by the request; the CJEU only interprets EU law.
• Revision to the VwGH open → discretion (Art 267(2) TFEU; Lyckeskog, C-99/00); duty only at last instance (Art 267(3); CILFIT, 283/81).
• No party right to a reference.
• CJEU neither annuls nor interprets national law ('precludes legislation such as…'); Art 263: EU acts only.

cards.q: Case — Lipa beer: Czech brewery Lipa lawfully makes and sells in Czechia a lager with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'; Austrian importer Hopfenhandel sells it in supermarkets and petrol-station shops. Austrian Beer Act: § 3 – 'Bier' only if brewed solely from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer may be sold at petrol stations. No EU harmonisation. An Austrian authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both. Austria invokes consumer expectations, health (rice beer 'less healthy') and drink-driving. On a reference, the Court of Justice rules that Art 34 and 36 TFEU preclude legislation such as § 3. (f) What must the Landesverwaltungsgericht now do, and what does the ruling mean beyond this case? (1 point)
cards.a:
Disapply § 3 itself and annul the fine to that extent.
• Primacy: no waiting for legislature/VfGH (Simmenthal, 106/77).
• Beyond: binds referring court, de facto all courts/authorities, ex tunc; Austria must amend § 3, else Art 258 TFEU.

cards.q: Case — Night work directive: The (fictional, valid) Night Work Directive, deadline 1 March 2026, Art 3: Member States ensure that night workers in hospitals and emergency services get from their employer at least 25% extra per night hour. Valdoria transposed nothing; its courts read § 12 Working Time Act ('appropriate' night compensation) as 10%. Anna, a night nurse at Medicor GmbH, a hospital owned by a private investment fund and (like every hospital) licensed and supervised by the Ministry, is paid 10%. She sues Medicor for 25% relying on Art 3. (a) Advise Anna. (4 points)
cards.a:
Anna cannot rely on Art 3 against Medicor: no horizontal direct effect, and Medicor is no emanation of the State.
• Art 3 is clear, precise, unconditional (beneficiary, debtor, 25% minimum; Van Gend en Loos, 26/62); deadline expired, no transposition (Ratti, 148/78) → only vertical direct effect.
• Art 288(3) TFEU binds only Member States; a directive cannot impose obligations on individuals (Marshall I, 152/84; Faccini Dori, C-91/92).
• Medicor: privately owned; licence and general supervision ≠ State control or special powers (Foster, C-188/89; Farrell, C-413/15).
• Charter: Art 31 grants no night allowance (unlike paid leave, Bauer, C-569/16).
• Instead: consistent interpretation of § 12 (Von Colson; Marleasing) or Francovich against Valdoria.

cards.q: Case — Night work directive: The (fictional, valid) Night Work Directive, deadline 1 March 2026, Art 3: Member States ensure that night workers in hospitals and emergency services get from their employer at least 25% extra per night hour. Valdoria transposed nothing; its courts read § 12 Working Time Act ('appropriate' night compensation) as 10%. Ben, a paramedic, works for Valdorian Rescue AG: shares wholly held by the regions, statutory exclusive 112 ambulance service, tariffs and supervisory board set by the Minister, crews may use blue lights and enter private premises. He is paid 10%. (b) Advise Ben. Does the private-law form matter? (3 points)
cards.a:
Ben can rely on Art 3 and claim 25% since 1 March 2026: Rescue AG is an emanation of the State; its AG form is irrelevant.
• Directives bind the State in any capacity, incl. as employer (Marshall I, 152/84), and all its bodies (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88).
• Emanation, whatever its legal form: State control, OR public-interest task with special powers – alternatives (Foster, C-188/89; Farrell, C-413/15).
• Both met: regional ownership, board, tariffs; 112 monopoly, blue lights, entry rights.
• Court disapplies the 10% reading (Simmenthal).

cards.q: Case — Night work directive: The (fictional, valid) Night Work Directive, deadline 1 March 2026, Art 3: Member States ensure that night workers in hospitals and emergency services get from their employer at least 25% extra per night hour. Valdoria transposed nothing; its courts read § 12 Working Time Act ('appropriate' night compensation) as 10%. The labour court has held that Anna, a nurse at the private hospital Medicor, cannot invoke Art 3 directly against her employer. (c) (i) What must the court nevertheless do with § 12? (ii) Would it change if § 12 read 'an allowance of 10% of the hourly wage'? (3 points)
cards.a:
(i) Read 'appropriate' as at least 25%, even against settled case law; (ii) a fixed 10% → contra legem: Anna loses and must sue Valdoria.
• Indirect effect: interpret national law as far as possible in light of the directive (Von Colson, 14/83; Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU), also between private parties and for earlier law (Marleasing, C-106/89).
• Settled case law must change (DI, C-441/14).
• Limits: no contra legem (Impact, C-268/06), no criminal liability (Kolpinghuis, 80/86).
• (ii) → Francovich damages from Valdoria.

cards.q: Case — Night work directive: The (fictional, valid) Night Work Directive, deadline 1 March 2026, Art 3: Member States ensure that night workers in hospitals and emergency services get from their employer at least 25% extra per night hour. Valdoria transposed nothing; its courts read § 12 Working Time Act ('appropriate' night compensation) as 10%. Art 7: on employer insolvency, a guarantee institution, organised and financed (public funds or employer levies) as each Member State decides, pays outstanding Art 3 allowances, possibly only for the last three months. Valdoria set up none. Clara's private employer became insolvent on 1 September 2026; her June–August allowances are unrecoverable. She sues Valdoria. (d) Advise Clara. (4 points)
cards.a:
Not on Art 7 directly (the debtor is not identified), but she wins Francovich damages against Valdoria.
• No direct effect against the State: Art 7 leaves organisation and financing of the guarantor open, so the State is not the debtor (Francovich, C-6/90).
• Basis: State liability inherent in the Treaties, effet utile, Art 4(3) TEU – not Art 340(2) TFEU (Union liability).
• Brasserie du Pêcheur (C-46/93): (1) rule confers rights, content identifiable ✓; (2) sufficiently serious – non-transposition per se (Dillenkofer, C-178/94) ✓; (3) direct causal link – June–August within the three-month limit ✓.
• Before Valdorian courts, under national rules respecting equivalence and effectiveness.

cards.topic: EU Institutions II — Council, Parliament, other bodies
cards.q: OLP on an Art 114 TFEU proposal: at first reading the EP adopts 30 amendments, which the Commission accepts by altering its proposal. In the Council (27 Member States), 16 states with 64.5% of the population vote to approve the EP's position, 4 (16%) vote against and 7 (19.5%) abstain. Is the EP's position approved, and what happens next? (2 points)
cards.a:
Not approved: 16 states suffice, but 64.5% < 65% of population; abstentions count like 'no' → the 11 non-supporters (35.5%) block.
• Art 16(4) TEU: ≥ 55% and ≥ 15 members + 65% population; blocking minority ≥ 4 members.
• QMV suffices – Commission accepted the amendments (Art 293(2) TFEU); otherwise unanimity (Art 293(1)).
• Next: Council's own first-reading position (Art 294(5) TFEU).

cards.q: OLP: the Council communicates its first-reading position to the EP (720 MEPs) on 15 September 2027. On 6 December 2027, 352 MEPs vote to reject it, 318 vote against and 30 abstain; nothing else happens before the deadline. What is the result? What if 365 MEPs had voted to reject? (2 points)
cards.a:
Rejection fails (needs 361 = majority of component members) → act deemed adopted in the Council's wording; with 365 → deemed not adopted.
• Art 294(7) TFEU: within three months (+1, Art 294(14)) approval or silence → adopted; rejection only by component majority.
• 352 > 318 is irrelevant – not votes cast (Art 231) but 361 of 720.
• Then publication (Art 297(1)).

cards.q: The Commission proposes a 'Directive on sustainable urban tourism' under Art 195(2) TFEU obliging all Member States to cap short-term holiday rentals at 5% of the housing stock in every district with a UNESCO site; its sole aim is preserving historic centres and residents' quality of life. What competence does the Union have, and is Art 195(2) TFEU a valid basis? Could Art 114 or Art 352 TFEU be used instead? (3 points)
cards.a:
No legal basis: tourism is a supporting competence excluding harmonisation; Art 114/352 TFEU cannot circumvent that.
• Conferral: every act needs a legal basis (Art 5(1)–(2) TEU); type from Art 2–6 TFEU, basis from the policy chapter (Art 2(6)).
• Art 6(d), 2(5) TFEU: no harmonisation; Art 195(2) excludes it – a uniform 5% cap harmonises.
• Art 114: needs a genuine internal-market aim; no circumventing exclusions (Tobacco Advertising, C-376/98).
• Art 352(3): no harmonisation where excluded.
• If adopted → annulment (Art 263 TFEU).

cards.q: An Art 114 TFEU proposal (OLP) obliges online short-term rental platforms to send booking data to national authorities in one EU format. Within eight weeks, reasoned opinions alleging a breach of subsidiarity arrive from the unicameral parliaments of Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Hungary, Portugal, Malta, Greece and Latvia, the Austrian Bundesrat and the Dutch Eerste Kamer. Does subsidiarity apply, and what follows? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes (shared competence); 18 of 54 votes = one third → yellow card: review, no veto.
• Art 5(3) TEU: outside exclusive competence; internal market shared (Art 4(2)(a) TFEU).
• Protocol No 2: eight weeks (Art 6); two votes per parliament, one per chamber (Art 7(1)) → 16 + 2.
• Art 7(2): Commission maintains, amends or withdraws (reasons); orange card (Art 7(3)) needs 28.

cards.q: The platform regulation (Art 114 TFEU) is adopted unchanged despite a yellow card and published in the Official Journal on 2 May 2028. The Danish Folketing still considers that it breaches subsidiarity. How can the matter reach the Court, and by when? Could the Committee of the Regions sue? How intensive is the review? (2 points)
cards.a:
Denmark sues (or notifies for the Folketing) at the Court of Justice by 26 July 2028; CoR cannot; marginal review.
• Art 8 Protocol No 2; Art 263(2) TFEU.
• Two months (Art 263(6)) from end of 14th day after publication + 10 days distance.
• CoR only if consultation required; Art 114: EESC only.
• Reasons and manifest error only (Philip Morris, C-547/14).

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: Do you agree? Brenland 'transposes' a directive (deadline 1 June 2026) by an unpublished internal ministry circular telling regional authorities to apply its noise limits; the Minister may amend it at any time. Brenland: 'Art 288(3) TFEU leaves us the choice of form and methods, so we have complied.' (1 point)
cards.a:
No – Brenland has not transposed the directive.
• Art 288(3) TFEU: the chosen form needs unquestionable binding force, clarity and publicity; mere administrative practice is not enough (Commission v Belgium, 102/79).
• Consequences: Art 258 TFEU, direct effect, Francovich.

cards.topic: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy
cards.q: A delegated act is notified on 2 March 2026; the basic act allows an objection within two months (extendable by two). On 28 April 2026 the EP (720 MEPs) votes on an objection: 351 for, 290 against, 40 abstentions. The Council does not object. Can the delegated act enter into force? (1 point)
cards.a:
Yes – an EP objection needs a majority of component members (361 of 720), not of votes cast.
• Art 290(2) TFEU: EP by component majority, Council by QMV (unlike Art 231).
• Enters into force when the period expires.

cards.q: Lumerian MPs challenge the (fictional) E-Prescription Regulation on cross-border e-prescriptions (Art 114 TFEU) before the Lumerian Constitutional Court. Without a reference, it declares the Regulation 'not applicable in Lumeria': (i) Art 168(7) TFEU reserves health services to the Member States → ultra vires; (ii) pharmacists' self-administration is part of Lumeria's constitutional identity. Assess the ruling from the CJEU's perspective and name the national 'constitutional reservation' doctrines. (3 points)
cards.a:
The ruling breaches EU law: only the CJEU rules on validity and competence; identity (Art 4(2) TEU) is an EU-law question to be referred.
• Primacy also over constitutions (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70); no national invalidation (Foto-Frost, 314/85); last instance → duty to refer (Art 267(3) TFEU).
• Identity doubts → refer (RS, C-430/21); unilateral rulings → infringement (Commission v Poland, C-448/23; Art 258 TFEU).
• BVerfG doctrines: rights (Solange), ultra vires (Maastricht, Honeywell, PSPP), identity (Lisbon).
• Even Honeywell demands a prior reference and a manifest excess – missing here.

cards.q: Member State Kalmaria has lost an infringement case before the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice. Its government announces that it will (a) appeal to the full Court, (b) require the Kalmarian judge to disclose his vote and publish a dissenting opinion, and (c) recall him and appoint a 'more loyal' judge for the rest of his term. (d) In a new infringement case assigned to a five-judge chamber, Kalmaria requests the Grand Chamber with its own judge sitting. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Only the Grand Chamber request (d) succeeds; (a)–(c) breach the Treaties and Statute.
• (a) No appeal: appeals lie only against General Court decisions (Art 256(1) TFEU); comply (Art 260(1)).
• (b) Deliberations stay secret (Art 35 Statute): no votes, no dissents.
• (c) Judges are independent, not delegates (Art 19(2) TEU; six-year term, Art 253 TFEU); removal only by unanimous opinion of judges and Advocates General (Art 6 Statute).
• (d) A party Member State may demand the Grand Chamber (Art 16(3) Statute), not its own judge (Art 18(4)).

cards.q: Ostravia has failed to transpose an EU directive. Neighbouring Westmark, whose companies compete with Ostravian ones, wants to submit the dispute to an international arbitral tribunal under a bilateral treaty between the two states. May it? (1 point)
cards.a:
No: Art 344 TFEU forbids settling disputes on the interpretation or application of the Treaties by any other method (MOX Plant, C-459/03).
• Westmark must use Art 259 TFEU, bringing the matter before the Commission first.

cards.q: Ostravia notified no measures transposing the Data Centre Directive (fictitious, adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure) and ignored the Commission's reasoned opinion. The Commission sues and asks the Court to impose both a lump sum and a daily penalty payment already in this first judgment. (i) May the Court combine both? (ii) What changes if Ostravia fully transposes after the reasoned-opinion deadline but before judgment? (2 points)
cards.a:
(i) Yes, under Art 260(3) TFEU; (ii) the breach is still declared, but only a lump sum remains.
• (i) Total or partial non-notification of a legislative directive (Commission v Belgium, C-543/17); combined in Commission v Spain, C-658/19; capped at the Commission's amount.
• (ii) Breach assessed at the reasoned-opinion deadline; penalty is coercive and lapses, lump sum punishes the past (Commission v Romania, C-549/18).

cards.q: Case — Trivolan: Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious; Parliament and Council, 2019) the Commission decides on renewal of approvals of active substances by implementing regulation after an EFSA assessment, and must first let the applicants comment on EFSA's conclusions; if renewal is refused, Member States must withdraw all national authorisations of products containing the substance. Feldmann GmbH was one of three joint applicants for renewal of trivolan. Without forwarding EFSA's conclusions, the Commission refused renewal by implementing regulation of 12 March 2026 (the 'Trivolan Regulation'), published in the OJ on 16 March 2026. Gartenwelt AG, a garden-centre chain selling many trivolan products, is also affected. Do Feldmann and Gartenwelt have standing to bring an action for annulment? (5 points)
cards.a:
Feldmann has standing as directly and individually concerned (Art 263(4), second limb, TFEU); Gartenwelt, one of an open class of retailers, has none.
• Reviewable act: binding Commission implementing regulation (Art 263(1)); neither company is privileged or addressee, so limb 2 or 3 of Art 263(4).
• Limb 3 doubtful: 'regulatory act' = non-legislative act of general application (Inuit, C-583/11 P), but national withdrawals are implementing measures (T&L Sugars, C-456/13 P).
• Direct concern: it refuses Feldmann's own application; Member States must withdraw without discretion.
• Individual concern (Plaumann, 25/62): closed group of three applicants fixed before adoption, plus a procedural guarantee, the right to comment (Timex, 264/82).
• Gartenwelt: affected only objectively as a retailer; national courts and a reference instead (Art 267; Foto-Frost, 314/85; UPA, C-50/00 P; Art 19(1) TEU).

cards.q: Case — Trivolan: The Commission's implementing regulation refusing renewal of the approval of the plant-protection substance trivolan was adopted on 12 March 2026 and published in the Official Journal on 16 March 2026. On 13 March an informal Commission e-mail told Feldmann GmbH, one of three applicants for renewal; its in-house lawyer thinks the annulment action was due by 13 May. External counsel plans to file on 5 June 2026. Before which court, and is 5 June in time? (2 points)
cards.a:
General Court (Art 256(1) TFEU); 5 June is in time: the period ends 9 June 2026.
• Art 263(6): two months from publication; knowledge counts only absent publication or notification; an e-mail is neither.
• GC RoP: 16 March + 14 days = 30 March (Art 59); + two months = 30 May (Art 58); + 10 days distance (Art 60) = Tuesday 9 June.

cards.q: Case — Trivolan: Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious; Parliament and Council, 2019), which governs only use and marketing within the Union, the Commission renews approvals by implementing regulation after an EFSA assessment and must first let applicants comment on EFSA's conclusions. Feldmann GmbH, one of three applicants, admissibly challenges the implementing regulation refusing renewal of trivolan. It argues: (i) it could never comment on EFSA's conclusions; (ii) the regulation also bans exports of trivolan to third countries; (iii) total refusal is disproportionate, as limiting use to closed greenhouses would suffice. Which grounds of annulment apply, and with what prospects? (3 points)
cards.a:
(i) essential procedural requirement, (ii) lack of competence, (iii) infringement of the Treaties (proportionality); (i), (ii) likely succeed, (iii) is weak.
• Art 263(2) TFEU: four grounds; misuse of powers not in issue.
• (i) Right to comment (cf. Art 41(2)(a) Charter) is essential; annulment if the outcome might have differed.
• (ii) Implementing act may not amend or supplement the basic act (Art 291(2) TFEU, Art 13(2) TEU): export ban ultra vires, severable.
• (iii) Art 5(4) TEU, but wide discretion plus precautionary principle (Pfizer, T-13/99): only manifest error.

cards.q: Case — Trivolan: The Commission refused renewal of the approval of the plant-protection substance trivolan by implementing regulation (the 'Trivolan Regulation'); Member States then had to withdraw all national authorisations of trivolan products. On 1 March 2027 the General Court annuls the Trivolan Regulation on an action by Feldmann GmbH, an applicant for renewal, because the applicants were not allowed to comment on EFSA's conclusions as the basic regulation requires. The Commission argues that the regulation stays in force while it appeals and that it may afterwards simply re-adopt the same text. Assess. (2 points)
cards.a:
First argument right, second wrong: a General Court annulment of a regulation takes effect only once the appeal period expires or an appeal is dismissed (Art 60(2) Statute).
• Then void ex tunc, erga omnes (Art 264(1) TFEU); effects may be maintained (Art 264(2)).
• Art 266 TFEU: comply with operative part and grounds; resume the procedure, hear the applicants, decide anew (refusal still possible).

cards.q: Case — Trivolan: Feldmann GmbH has brought an admissible action before the General Court against the Commission's implementing regulation refusing renewal of the approval of the substance trivolan. The refusal applies Art 4(7) of the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious), a 2019 legislative act of Parliament and Council requiring refusal whenever a substance is 'potentially' endocrine-disrupting, without assessing exposure. Feldmann argues Art 4(7) is disproportionate. The Commission replies that the 2019 regulation can no longer be challenged and that companies cannot attack legislative acts anyway. Assess. (2 points)
cards.a:
Both objections fail: Feldmann may plead illegality of Art 4(7) under Art 277 TFEU despite the expired Art 263(6) time limit.
• 'Any party', any act of general application, legislative acts included; Art 263(2) grounds.
• Conditions: pending action; contested act applies Art 4(7).
• Purpose: those unable to sue directly (Simmenthal v Commission, 92/78).
• Effect inter partes: Art 4(7) inapplicable, contested act annulled.

cards.q: Case — Trivolan: Under the Plant Protection Regulation (fictitious; Parliament and Council, 2019) the Commission must approve or refuse a new active substance by implementing regulation within six months of EFSA's conclusions. Feldmann GmbH applied in 2024 for approval of trivolan-S; EFSA concluded favourably in July 2025, but nothing has happened. Feldmann's formal letter calling on the Commission to decide was received on 2 April 2026; by 15 June 2026 there is no reply. The Commission says Feldmann cannot sue, because the act sought would be a regulation, not an act addressed to Feldmann. Is an action admissible, and until when? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes: action for failure to act before the General Court (Arts 265, 256(1) TFEU), to be lodged by 12 August 2026.
• Art 265(3) read like Art 263(4): direct and individual concern suffices (T. Port, C-68/95); Feldmann applied for the approval.
• Duty since January 2026; call 2 April; silence to 2 June; + two months + 10 days = 12 August.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Directive 2025/88 (fictitious) requires Member States to make holiday-rental hosts record guests' identity and dates of stay and send them to the police, leaving the retention period to the Member States. Austria's Guest Data Act lets the police keep all guests' data for ten years. Marta, a Slovenian host in Graz, invokes Arts 7 and 8 Charter. Austria says the Charter does not apply: the Act is national law and the ten-year period a purely national choice. Is the Charter applicable? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes: transposing the directive, including the discretion it leaves, is 'implementing Union law' (Art 51(1) Charter).
• Charter binds Member States whenever EU law governs (Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10).
• Using a discretion conferred by EU law stays within it (N.S., C-411/10; Tele2 Sverige, C-203/15).
• National form and Marta's nationality are irrelevant; national rights may apply too (Art 53 Charter; Melloni, C-399/11).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Karl, an Austrian journalist, is convicted under the Austrian Criminal Code of defaming his home town's mayor in a local newspaper. On appeal he invokes freedom of expression under Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights. Can he? (1 point)
cards.a:
No: national criminal defamation proceedings do not implement Union law (Art 51(1) Charter).
• Art 51(2) Charter, Art 6(1) TEU: no extension of EU competences; a sufficient link is needed (Siragusa, C-206/12). Karl relies on Art 10 ECHR instead.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Austria's Guest Data Act (transposing a fictitious EU directive against terrorism and serious crime) obliges holiday-rental hosts to send every guest's identity and dates of stay to the police, who keep them for ten years; any officer may consult them for any offence without prior authorisation by a court or independent body. Assuming the Charter applies, is this a justified limitation of Articles 7 and 8 Charter? Apply Article 52(1) Charter. (3 points)
cards.a:
No: legal basis, essence and aim are fine, but the regime exceeds what is strictly necessary.
• Interference with private life (Art 7) and data protection (Art 8) (Digital Rights Ireland, C-293/12).
• Art 52(1): (1) provided for by law: statute; (2) essence untouched: only identity and dates; (3) general-interest aim: fighting serious crime; (4) proportionality: strictly necessary.
• (4) fails: every guest without any link to a threat, ten years undifferentiated, access for any offence without prior review (Tele2 Sverige, C-203/15; Ligue des droits humains, C-817/19).

cards.q: Case — Mountain guides: The Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 (fictitious) lets only members of a private association of mostly self-employed guides guide paying clients on Tyrolean glaciers; membership requires a recognised diploma and two years' residence in Tyrol. Jana, a Czech guide with a Czech state diploma living and working in Brno, takes groups of Czech clients for a fee to the Stubai Glacier for about three weeks every winter; not living in Tyrol, she cannot become a member. Tyrol argues EU law does not apply, since Jana and all her clients are Czech. Does the Act restrict Jana's fundamental freedom? Examine scope and type of restriction. (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes: Art 56 TFEU applies although all are Czech; the residence condition is indirect nationality discrimination, compulsory membership a further obstacle.
• Services, not establishment: based in Brno, in Austria only temporarily, even if every winter (Gebhard, C-55/94; Schnitzer, C-215/01).
• Cross-border: guide travelling with her group (Commission v France, tourist guides, C-154/89).
• Restriction: anything impeding or making less attractive (Säger, C-76/90); residence favours Austrians, can nullify the freedom (Van Binsbergen, 33/74).
• Directive 2005/36: no compulsory membership (Art 6(a)).

cards.q: Case — Mountain guides: The Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 (fictitious) lets only members of a private association of mostly self-employed guides guide paying clients on Tyrolean glaciers; membership requires a recognised diploma and two years' residence in Tyrol. Jana, a Czech guide established in Brno, guides Czech clients for a fee on the Stubai Glacier about three weeks every winter but cannot become a member. Assume the Act restricts her freedom to provide services. Tyrol argues that glacier tours are dangerous and guides must know the local terrain and the mountain-rescue system. Can the restriction be justified? (3 points)
cards.a:
No: client safety is an overriding public-interest reason, but residence and compulsory membership are neither suitable nor necessary.
• Grounds: Arts 62, 52(1) TFEU need a genuine, sufficiently serious threat; the measure is not directly discriminatory, so overriding reasons such as safety apply (Säger; Gebhard).
• Suitability: residence proves no glacier knowledge, Jana guides there yearly: not consistent and systematic (Hartlauer, C-169/07).
• Necessity: prior declaration and qualification check (Directive 2005/36, Art 7(4)), rescue briefing, insurance; temporary registration (Art 6(a)).
• Burden on Austria: Art 56 infringed.

cards.q: Case — Mountain guides: The Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 (fictitious) lets only members of a guides' association requiring two years' residence in Tyrol guide on Tyrolean glaciers; assume this infringes Art 56 TFEU. The district authority fines Jana, a Czech guide established in Brno, EUR 2,000. On appeal, the Tyrolean Regional Administrative Court, whose decisions can be challenged before the VwGH and VfGH, believes only the VfGH can set aside a statute. How must it proceed, and may or must it refer to the Court of Justice? (2 points)
cards.a:
It must itself disapply the requirements and annul the fine; it may refer (Art 267(2) TFEU) but need not.
• Art 56 is directly effective (Van Binsbergen); every court sets aside conflicting law itself, without awaiting constitutional review (Simmenthal, 106/77; Melki, C-188/10).
• Appealable to the VwGH, even with leave, so no duty (Lyckeskog, C-99/00); the VwGH must refer unless CILFIT applies (Art 267(3)).

cards.q: Case — Mountain guides: Luca, an Italian with an Italian mountain-guide diploma recognised in Austria as equivalent, has lived in Innsbruck for three years and takes a salaried guide job with Alpin GmbH, a private company. Alpin's pay policy grants a 15% 'local training bonus' only to guides trained at the Tyrolean state guide academy, so Luca is refused it. Can Luca rely on EU law against Alpin GmbH? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes: Art 45 TFEU binds private employers (Angonese, C-281/98), and the bonus is unjustified indirect nationality discrimination.
• Art 45(2): no discrimination in pay and working conditions; horizontal (Walrave, 36/74; Bosman, C-415/93).
• Tyrolean training is mostly met by Austrians: indirect discrimination (O'Flynn, C-237/94).
• No objective justification: equivalent diploma, so the bonus rewards place, not competence.
• Also Reg 492/2011, Art 7(1), (4).

cards.q: Case — Mountain guides: Under the Tyrolean Mountain Guides Act 2025 (fictitious) only members of a private association of mostly self-employed guides may guide on Tyrolean glaciers; many clients come from other Member States. On its own initiative the association's general assembly adopts a binding 'fair tariff' of at least EUR 480 per guided glacier day; members who charge less are expelled and lose the right to guide. The Tyrolean government neither required nor approved it. Is the tariff compatible with EU competition law? Which provision, and what consequences? (3 points)
cards.a:
No: a decision by an association of undertakings fixing minimum prices, restrictive by object (Art 101(1)(a) TFEU), void (Art 101(2)).
• Undertakings: self-employed guides (Höfner, C-41/90; Pavlov, C-180/98); binding resolution = association decision (Wouters, C-309/99); not state conduct (contrast Arduino, C-35/99).
• By object: no effects analysis, no Wouters-type safety defence (Superleague, C-333/21); foreign clients: inter-state trade; Art 101(3) fails.
• Void ex tunc, expulsions unlawful; fines (up to 10% of members' turnover, Art 23(2) Reg 1/2003; or Austrian Cartel Court); damages (Courage, C-453/99).

cards.q: Case — Kovács: Eszter Kovács, a Hungarian national, moved to Vienna with her two children in January 2025. Since February 2025 she has worked 12 hours a week as a cleaner for a private firm (€520 a month); a municipal minimum-income benefit tops up her income. In March 2026 she applies for a Viennese rent subsidy for families, which the (fictitious) Vienna Housing Subsidy Act grants only to persons whose main residence has been in Austria for at least five years. The Magistrat refuses. Eszter appeals to the Verwaltungsgericht Wien, whose decisions can be challenged before the Verwaltungsgerichtshof (VwGH). (a) Is Eszter a 'worker' within Article 45 TFEU, and why does the examination start with Article 45 rather than Article 18 or 21 TFEU? (2 points)
cards.a:
Yes — she is a worker; Art 45 TFEU (lex specialis) comes first.
• Lawrie-Blum (66/85): services for and under another's direction, for remuneration; Hungarian in Austria = cross-border.
• 12 h/€520 is genuine and effective, not marginal and ancillary (Levin 53/81); social top-up irrelevant (Kempf 139/85).
• Art 18(1) TFEU applies 'without prejudice to any special provisions'; Art 21(1) is general → both subsidiary.

cards.q: Case — Kovács: Eszter Kovács, a Hungarian national, moved to Vienna with her two children in January 2025. Since February 2025 she has worked 12 hours a week as a cleaner for a private firm (€520 a month); a municipal minimum-income benefit tops up her income. In March 2026 she applies for a Viennese rent subsidy for families, which the (fictitious) Vienna Housing Subsidy Act grants only to persons whose main residence has been in Austria for at least five years. The Magistrat refuses. Eszter appeals to the Verwaltungsgericht Wien, whose decisions can be challenged before the Verwaltungsgerichtshof (VwGH). (b) Does the five-year residence requirement infringe Article 45 TFEU? Examine discrimination and justification. (3 points)
cards.a:
Yes — unjustified indirect discrimination on grounds of nationality (Art 45(2) TFEU).
• Rent subsidy = 'social advantage' (Art 7(2), housing Art 9 Reg 492/2011) → equal terms with nationals.
• Applies to all but more easily met by Austrians → indirect discrimination (O'Flynn C-237/94).
• Art 45(3) (public policy, security, health) does not fit; budgetary aims never justify; an overriding reason (genuine link) must be suitable and necessary.
• Working and paying taxes in Austria already proves integration (Commission v Netherlands C-542/09) → five years disproportionate.

cards.q: Case — Kovács: Eszter Kovács, a Hungarian national, has lived in Vienna since January 2025 and from February 2025 worked 12 hours a week as a cleaner (€520/month). Vienna refuses her a rent subsidy for families, which requires five years' main residence in Austria. In June 2026, after 16 months of work, her employer dismisses her for economic reasons; she registers with the AMS as a job-seeker. The Magistrat now argues that she is an economically inactive Union citizen who may be refused social assistance under Article 24(2) of Directive 2004/38 (Dano). (c) Is the Magistrat right? Would it differ if Eszter had never worked and lacked sufficient resources? (3 points)
cards.a:
No — she retains worker status and full equal treatment; had she never worked, she could be refused.
• Art 7(3)(b) Dir 2004/38: recorded involuntary unemployment after > 1 year of work + registered job-seeker → status kept (< 1 year: at least six months, Art 7(3)(c)).
